content: Potassium nitrate is a chemical compound with the formula KNO₃. It is a naturally occurring mineral that serves as a significant source of nitrogen. Historically, it has been a critical oxidizing agent in black powder gunpowder and was also used in various types of burning fuses, such as slow matches. Due to its ability to precipitate readily, urine was a major source of potassium nitrate from the Late Middle Ages through the 19th century, despite the malodorous methods involved in its extraction. Common names for potassium nitrate include saltpeter (from the Medieval Latin sal petrae, meaning stone salt or possibly Salt of Petra), nitrate of potash, and nitre. Sodium nitrate, a different nitrogen compound used in explosives and fertilizers, is sometimes referred to as Chile saltpeter. Potassium nitrate is the oxidizing component of black powder. Before the industrial-scale fixation of nitrogen via the Haber process, potassium nitrate was primarily obtained from deposits crystallizing on cave walls or from the decomposition of organic material. Dung heaps were a common source, as ammonia from the breakdown of urea and other nitrogenous materials underwent bacterial oxidation to produce nitrate. It was also used as a component in some fertilizers, providing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. There was a historical belief that potassium nitrate could induce impotence, and it was rumored to be included in institutional food, such as military rations, as an anaphrodisiac. However, potassium nitrate has no such properties. On the contrary, nitrates, including potassium nitrate, are effective in managing high blood pressure and are used medically to relieve angina. In traditional methods, potassium nitrate was produced by collecting urine, which was filtered through straw and allowed to sour for a year or more. The resulting chemical salts were washed out with water, filtered through wood ashes, and dried in the sun. The crystallized saltpeter was then combined with sulfur and charcoal to create black powder. Potassium nitrate could also be harvested from bat guano deposits in caves, a method traditionally used in Laos for manufacturing gunpowder for Bang Fai rockets. During the 19th century and up until World War I, potassium nitrate was produced industrially, initially via the Birkeland–Eyde process in 1905 and later from ammonia synthesized through the more efficient Haber process. The Haber process became critical during World War I, as it allowed Germany to produce nitrates for warfare despite being cut off from natural nitrate deposits in Chile, which were controlled by the British. Today, nearly all nitrates are produced using ammonia from the Haber process. Potassium nitrate has various applications. Historically, it was used as an anaphrodisiac, though this use is ineffective. It is also employed as a fertilizer, in amateur rocket propellants, and in fireworks, such as smoke bombs. In smoke bombs, a mixture of potassium nitrate and sugar produces a smoke cloud 600 times its own volume. The typical ratio for smoke bombs using sucrose (powdered sugar) and potassium nitrate is 40:60. This mixture can be used as is or consolidated into a lump by mixing it with water to form a paste and allowing it to dry overnight. In food preservation, potassium nitrate was once a common ingredient in salted meat, though its use has declined. In the European Union, it is designated as E252. It is also used in pre-rolled cigarettes to ensure an even burn of the tobacco. Additionally, potassium nitrate is the primary component (approximately 98%) of tree stump removers, as it accelerates the natural decomposition of the stump. It has also been used in the manufacture of ice cream and is found in some toothpastes for sensitive teeth. Recently, its use in toothpastes for treating dental hypersensitivity has increased significantly, although its effectiveness in addressing dental hypersensitivity has not been conclusively proven. Potassium nitrate is one of the three main components of black powder, along with powdered charcoal (primarily carbon) and sulfur, where it functions as an oxidizer.
